newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk Telekom sell-off given green light by court.
newsitem.headline: Turk Telekom sell-off given green light by court.

text.p: Turkey's constitutional court on Thursday gave the green light for the sale of Turk Telekom, the centrepiece of the government's privatisation plans, a court official said.
The Istanbul stock market reacted positively to the news, with the main index jumping 7.91 percent in afternoon trading.
The constitutional court rejected most of a challenge by 116 opposition MPs to the sell-off. "This decision will not block the sale of Telekom shares," a court official said.
The Islamist-led government hopes to raise $3.5 billion from the telecommunications sale, which had been halted three times by the constitutional court since 1993.
Transport Minister Omer Barutcu told Reuters 10 percent of Telekom would be sold in the first tranche.
"Ten percent will be issued to assess our market condition at that time," he said, noting that under the privatisation plan 49 percent of Telekom is to be sold.
A consortium headed by Goldman Sachs was last month appointed to advise on the sell-off.
Turkey's privatisation programme has moved sluggishly since its inception 10 years ago, raising total revenues of just $3 billion despite bold government forecasts each year.

But State Minister Ufuk Soylemez last week fuelled expectations of accelerated sales, announcing Turkey would prepare at least $750-800 million worth of sell-offs during January, after only $300 million in the whole of 1996.
"With this decision by the constitutional court the way is opened for the rest of privatisation," Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller told reporters.

Recent sales of a bank and tyre and cement factories and the leasing of port facilities have boosted government hopes of reaching a target of $5 billion from sell-offs this year. That figure does not include any revenues from Telekom.
Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has dropped his opposition to privatisation since he formed a coalition with free-marketeer Ciller last June.
The government is planning to open tenders in the first quarter for the partial sale of state refiner Tupras and petroleum products distributor Petrol Ofisi.

Erbakan said last week the 1996 budget deficit would be 1,200 trillion lira ($10.6 billion), compared with 316.6 trillion a year earlier. Parliament last month approved for 1997 a zero-deficit budget based on expectations of considerable revenues from privatisations.
